newsitem.title: ALBANIA: ALBANIA MOURNS REFUGEES, ITALY PREPARES FORCE.
newsitem.headline: ALBANIA MOURNS REFUGEES, ITALY PREPARES FORCE.

text.p: Albania declared a day of mourning on Monday for refugees drowned in a shipwreck off Italy, battering Rome's image as it organised a multinational force to protect aid to the chaos-torn country.

President Sali Berisha, whose government approved the armed mission expected to number 2,500 troops and police, ordered Albania's flag -- red with a double-headed black eagle -- to fly at half mast across the nation in a sign of respect.

He called for a minute's silence at midday (1000 GMT) and asked motorists to blare horns to mourn the 83 people whom Tirana says drowned when their crammed vessel sank in the Adriatic after a collision with an Italian patrol ship.
Tirana angrily demanded an investigation as Friday's sinking cast a shadow over Italy's leadership of a U.N.-approved force to protect aid shipments to the lawless Balkan country.

Survivors accused Italy of deliberately ramming the vessel as part of a policy to halt a flood of 13,000 refugees from Albania, where protests against the collapse of savings schemes erupted into armed revolt in mid-March.

"This couldn't have come at a worse time," one diplomat said as Italy's image in Albania switched from selfless to selfish. "Let's hope that we don't go into a tunnel without an end. It's a very unpredictable situation."
Thirty-four people survived the sinking and only four bodies were recovered.

Passions ran highest in Vlore, the southern port from which the ill-fated Russian-built vessel left and one of the two main ports that the Italian-led force is due to secure as a bridgehead for relief supplies.
"I warn Italian soldiers not to come to Vlore, otherwise they will be killed," said Aida, 35, a woman who attended a rally by about 7,000 people to mourn the dead.

Advance units of the multinational force are expected to arrive in coming days, but some diplomats suggested it might start by securing Tirana airport and the northern port of Durres before moving to Vlore later.
"They may leave Vlore for last. Perhaps with no Italians," one diplomat said.

Despite the uproar over the sinking, Albania's parliament, dominated by Berisha's rightist Democratic Party, voted 97 to one to accept the force to ease the country's worst crisis since the collapse of communism in 1990.
Italy said it would press ahead with assembling the force. "I hope that the mission can leave immediately because Italy has been ready since March 17-18," Prime Minister Romano Prodi said.
Diplomats said the force, expected to include units from Italy, France, Greece, Spain and Portugal, could take days, perhaps even a couple of weeks, to organise.
Much of southern Albania, including Vlore, remains outside government control after mayhem earlier this month when arms depots were looted. Most foreigners were evacuated by helicopter or ship.
The violence in the once-proudly atheist state apparently slackened over Easter. The state ATA news agency reported only one shooting death on Sunday.

Italy and Greece fear the Albanian crisis could trigger a fresh massive wave of illegal immigration, as happened in 1991 and 1992 after the ruthless Stalinist regime which ruled for 45 years collapsed.
Italy, which invaded Albania in 1914 and 1939, sent 500 unarmed troops to Albania for two years from 1991 to help to distribute food and medicine.
